tn.quote: (c) léǹ « gourde » … Nous pouvons alors apercevoir qu’en position de noyau, le ton haut (H) se synchronise avec la voyelle e. Il en est de même pour la consonne nasale n dont le port du ton bas (B) se matérialise par la liaison entre deux positions de représentation de la syllabe: la position tonale et la position segmentale. … - des positions coda traversées par des tons. Ce qui nous amène à ne pas limiter l’unité porteuse du ton à la voyelle ni à l’étendre à la syllabe, mais à la more, une unité intermédiaire entre les deux entités phonologiques évoquées.
tn.translation: (c) léǹ 'gourd' … We can then see that in nucleus position the high tone (H) is synchronised with the vowel e. The same holds for the nasal consonant n, whose bearing of the low tone (B) is materialised by the link between two positions of the syllable representation: the tonal position and the segmental position. … - coda positions crossed by tones. This leads us not to limit the tone-bearing unit to the vowel nor to extend it to the syllable, but to the mora, a unit intermediate between the two phonological entities mentioned.
tn.cite: Kouraogo, Yacouba & Abdoul-Rassid Bagagnan. 2026. Internal Organization and Syllabic Governance in Moba / Structure et gouvernement syllabiques en moba. Uirtus (Université de Lomé) 6(2), 572-593. doi:10.59384/uirtus.aug2026.n291

tn.quote: Vietnamese and Muong are both monosyllabic languages with one phonemic tone occurring on each syllable (word). … Muong has a system of five phonemic tones: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, and high-mid level. In words with a final stop (p, t, ch, c), this five-way contrast is neutralized to a two-way contrast, the two being phonetically high rising and high-mid level. … [fn. 7] Words with high-mid level tone without a final stop (p, t, ch, c) have a final glottal stop as an integral part of the tone, whether there is another final consonant or not.

tn.note: Five tones, one on each syllable: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, high-mid level (with a final glottal stop); before final stops only high rising and high-mid level occur.

5427.idn: Name in the source: Naki (Mashi variety in Lower Fungom; Mekaf variety; earlier literature 'Mekaf'); family in the source: (Eastern) Beboid; Bantoid

tones: falling contours, e.g. nya᷆m 'animals', bâm '2.my' (not counted; unit vs. level-sequence analysis left open)
rising contours, e.g. ŋku᷅ŋ 'chief' (not counted; fewer than falling)
tn.quote: There is clear evidence for the presence of four tone levels in Naki, as exemplified by the set of words gí ‘ egg’, lī ‘ tongue’, shè ‘ fowl’, and mȕ ‘ person’. The treatment of mȕ as super low as opposed to gí as super high reflects an impression regarding relative frequency, though this is not yet well substantiated. Contour tones are also frequently encountered, and some examples include ŋku᷅ŋ ‘ chief’, nya᷆m ‘ animals’, and bâm ‘ 2. my’. As suggested by these examples, the inventory of falling tones appears to be larger than that of rising tones.
tn.cite: Good, Jeff, Jesse Lovegren, Jean Patrick Mve, Carine Nganguep Tchiemouo, Rebecca Voll & Pierpaolo Di Carlo. 2011. The languages of the Lower Fungom region of Cameroon: Grammatical overview. Africana Linguistica 17: 101-164.
tn.note: Four tone levels (super high to super low: gí, lī, shè, mȕ) plus frequent falling and some rising contours, not further analysed; earlier work assumed three levels. Nothing on word stress. Checked against the source (tone consistency check round 3, 2026-09-24): system level-and-contour -> level-or-register (p. 154, sec. 3.7.2.3 'Tones'; p. 111, sec. 3.1 general caveat).

tn.quote: Shintani (2016) analyzes Matu as having only two lexical tones (H and M). … Other languages permit both Rises and Falls, such as Mizo, Kuki-Thaadow, Falam, Khumi, and Matu. … To account for the often constrained realization of contour tones, researchers consider two options: (1) level tones are underlying and may be realized as contours in some contexts (finally), or (2) contours are underlying and may be reduced to level tones in some contexts (non-finally). Shintani’s (2016) analysis of Matu involves the former—Pre-pausal H and M on smooth syllables are realized as Rises.

tn.translation: Sketch of the phoneme system of Gaopo Miao. Gaopo speech belongs to the Northern vernacular of the Huishui sub-dialect of the Chuanqiandian dialect of Miao. The Northern vernacular is mainly spoken at Gaopo in Guiyang city, Yangchang in Huishui county, and Tangbao and Pingfa in Guiding county; 50,000 speakers. This material takes the Miao of Jiading village, Gaopo Miao township, Guiyang, Guizhou as representative. ... tn.quote: There are two basic tones in Odual, low and high, plus a downstep. In this paper only the high and the downstep are marked. The high tone is marked ('), while the downstep is marked (6·6) with an arrow pointing downwards between two high-toned moras. In general, the low tone is not marked for the sake of convenience. … Tonally, the first person singular and first person plural exclusive subject pronouns have a high tone pattern, i.e. all moras are high toned; … while the second person singular subject pronoun has a high-downstepped-high tone pattern.

tn.note: Two level tones, low and high, plus a downstepped high between two highs; tones are assigned mora by mora (a long vowel is one syllable of two moras); tone also marks grammatical distinctions.

5434.idn: Name in the source: Ksingmul (autonym ksiiŋ muul; known as Xinh Mun in Vietnam; official Lao form Singmoon; local exonym Puak); family in the source: Austroasiatic ('a typical Austroasiatic sesquisyllabic language')

tones: high-rising-pitch tone ('more marked', written with acute)
tn.quote: Another interesting feature that remains to be explained in terms of the history of the language is the existence of a two-way tone contrast on many word pairs in Ksingmul – a mid- to low-pitch tone that is more prominent, and a high-rising-pitch tone that is more marked. Contrasting pairs include: hreɲ ‘intestine’ and hréɲ ‘bamboo grub’, tal ‘downstream’ and tál ‘to touch, to disturb’, kaw ‘raw’ and káw ‘unpounded rice’ and ruu ‘to burn’ and rúu ‘to hurry’. Some borrowed Tai words have a high rising pitch, providing lexical contrast with a native word …
tn.cite: Badenoch, Nathan. 2022. Speaking Like a Ghost: Registers of Intimacy and Incompatibility in the Forests of Northern Laos. Journal of the Siam Society 110(1): 103-150.

tn.note: Two-way lexical tone contrast on many word pairs: an unmarked mid-to-low tone vs a marked high-rising tone (e.g. hreɲ 'intestine' / hréɲ 'bamboo grub'); a brief remark, no fuller analysis given.

5435.idn: Name in the source: Red Gelao (autonym transcribed va35 nt-31 [Na Khe]; u33 wei55 [Malipo]); family in the source: a form of the Gelao language, 'smallest member of the Gelao complex', close to / distant sister of SW Gelao (White Gelao); Proto-Kra reconstructions after Ostapirat 2000…

tones: B tone (pitch shape identical to D tone)
tn.quote: 2. Tones. There are four tones in Red Gelao. … The tonal system of Red Gelao shows no split in vocabulary descended from the proto A, B, and D tones and has such a split between the high and low set only in the proto-tone category C, but there is quite a lot of tone change in context especially when lexical items in the C category occur in a compound when they often change from 13 to 35 tone values. Red Gelao retains the Gelao development that original B tone vocabulary has a pitch shape identical to that found in D tone vocabulary, cf. Ostapirat (2000:80).
tn.cite: Edmondson, Jerold A. & Li Jinfang. [2003/2004]. Red Gelao, the most endangered form of the Gelao language. Unpublished ms. (Univ. of Texas at Arlington / Central Univ. of Nationalities), 6 pp. (Glottolog 317732; formerly ling.uta.edu/~).
tn.locator: sec. 2 'Tones', ms. pp. 2-3: heading and Table 1, paragraph
tn.note: Four lexical tones by proto-category: A, B (= D in pitch shape), C1, C2; forms show level 44 and contours 31, 13, 35; C-category 13 often becomes 35 in compounds; C tones keep glottal constriction.
